title: The Olive-Tree and the Fig-Tree
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: An Olive-tree taunted a Fig-tree with the loss of her leaves at a certain season of the year. "You," she said, "lose your leaves every autumn, and are bare till the spring: whereas I, as you see, remain green and flourishing all the year round."

Soon afterwards there came a heavy fall of snow, which settled on the leaves of the Olive so that she bent and broke under the weight; but the flakes fell harmlessly through the bare branches of the Fig, which survived to bear many another crop.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Olive-tree taunt the Fig-tree about?
options: Her small and unimpressive fruit
Her slow rate of growth
The loss of her leaves at a certain season
Her thin, weak branches

questions.prompt: According to the passage, when does the Fig-tree lose her leaves?
options: Every autumn
Every spring
Only in years of drought
Only when attacked by insects

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Olive-tree claim about herself?
options: That she grows taller than any other tree
That her fruit is the sweetest in the orchard
That she never needs water to survive
That she remains green and flourishing all the year round

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens soon after the Olive-tree's boast?
options: A drought strikes the region
A heavy fall of snow comes
A strong wind uproots several trees
A swarm of insects attacks the leaves

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Olive-tree because of the snow?
options: She sheds her leaves early to survive
She grows even more vigorously afterward
She bends and breaks under the weight of it
She is unaffected because of her thick trunk

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Fig-tree during the snowfall?
options: The snow falls harmlessly through her bare branches
She is also damaged, though less severely
She loses the last of her leaves permanently
She is protected by the nearby Olive-tree

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the very feature the Olive-tree mocked end up saving the Fig-tree?
options: The Fig-tree secretly grew stronger branches over the winter
The snow avoided the Fig-tree entirely by chance
The Fig-tree was planted in a more sheltered spot
Having no leaves means the snow has nothing to gather on and weigh the branches down

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the outcome suggest about the Olive-tree's boast?
options: The boast turned out to be completely accurate in every way
What seemed like an advantage turned out to make her vulnerable in a way the Fig-tree was not
The Fig-tree's loss of leaves was ultimately a greater weakness
Neither tree was actually affected by the season at all

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "taunted" mean in "An Olive-tree taunted a Fig-tree"?
options: Helped or supported
Warned or cautioned
Mocked or teased
Praised or admired

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: A trait that seems like a weakness in one season can turn into a real advantage in another
Trees that keep their leaves year-round are always the strongest
Snowfall is more dangerous to fruit trees than any other weather
Boasting about one's strengths always leads to misfortune

questions.prompt: According to the passage, until when does the Fig-tree remain bare?
options: Until midsummer
Until the following autumn
Until a new tree is planted
Until the spring

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what settles on the Olive-tree's leaves?
options: A layer of morning frost
A heavy fall of snow
A swarm of insects
A coating of dust

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fig-tree go on to do after surviving the snow?
options: She stops producing fruit for several years
She grows taller than the Olive-tree
She survives to bear many another crop
She is transplanted to a safer location

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Olive-tree's constant green leaves be seen as a disadvantage in this particular situation?
options: They give the snow something to collect on, adding weight the tree cannot bear
They attract more insects than the Fig-tree's leaves
They make the tree easier to spot and damage by storms
They require more water than the tree can find in winter

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what broader lesson about comparing strengths and weaknesses does the story suggest?
options: The tree with the most leaves is always the strongest overall
Weaknesses can never become strengths under any circumstances
Comparing two different trees is never a fair or useful exercise
An apparent weakness in one situation may become a hidden strength in another

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "flourishing" mean in "green and flourishing all the year round"?
options: Withering and dying slowly
Thriving and growing vigorously
Standing perfectly still
Changing color repeatedly

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Fig-tree mocks an Olive-tree for keeping her leaves too long
Both trees are equally damaged by a heavy snowfall
An Olive-tree mocks a Fig-tree for losing her leaves, but a snowfall breaks the Olive while the bare Fig survives unharmed
The Olive-tree and Fig-tree agree to share the same soil peacefully
